Series::logsumexp¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::logsumexp() const -> Series
Series::logsumexp(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::logsumexp(std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim) const -> Series

What It Does¶

logsumexp() reduces an axis by log(sum(exp(x))) — the log of the total of the exponentials.

Naively that reads “exponentiate, add up, take the log,” and naively it is unusable: for x around 1000, exp(x) is already past the top of float64 and the whole thing collapses to inf. logsumexp() is the stable version. It shifts by the maximum first:

m = max(x)                       (along the reduced axis)
logsumexp(x) = m + log(sum(exp(x - m)))

Every shifted exponent x - m is <= 0, so exp of it lies in (0, 1] and cannot overflow, while the largest term contributes exactly 1.

This is the normalizing constant of a softmax. softmax(x) = exp(x - logsumexp(x)), and a cross-entropy loss is logsumexp(logits) - logits[target]. Anywhere probabilities are carried as unnormalized log-scores, logsumexp() is how you total them without leaving log-space.

The no-argument form reduces the whole series to a scalar. The dim forms reduce one axis; keepdim controls whether that axis is kept as a length-1 dimension.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t, optional)

The axis to reduce. Negative values count from the back. Omitted: reduce everything to a scalar.

keepdim (bool, default false)

Keep the reduced axis as size 1 instead of removing it. Useful when the result is broadcast back against the input, as in x - x.logsumexp(dim, true) to build a log-softmax.

Returns¶

Series The reduced result. A scalar for the no-argument form; otherwise the input shape with dim removed (or kept as 1 when keepdim is set). Floating point.

Gradient¶

logsumexp() is differentiable, and its backward is the softmax of the input:

d/dx_k logsumexp(x) = exp(x_k) / sum_j exp(x_j) = softmax(x)_k

The gradients along the reduced axis are non-negative and sum to 1 — the upstream sensitivity is distributed across the inputs in proportion to how much each contributed to the total.

Examples¶

Example 1. A whole-series reduction to a scalar.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}).logsumexp(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=3.4076

log(e^1 + e^2 + e^3) = 3.4076.

Example 2. Reducing one axis of a matrix.

auto m = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});

std::cout << "dim 0: ";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, m.logsumexp(0));
std::cout << "\ndim 1: ";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, m.logsumexp(1));

Output¶

dim 0: Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[3.1269, 4.1269]
dim 1: Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[2.3133, 4.3133]

Example 3. keepdim keeps the reduced axis as size 1 for broadcasting back.

auto m = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});

std::cout << m.logsumexp(1, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[2.3132617],
  [4.3132617]]

Example 4. The stability that motivates the method. Every element is 1000; the naive x.exp().sum().log() overflows, logsumexp() returns the right answer.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1000.0, 1000.0, 1000.0}).logsumexp(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=1001.0986

1000 + log(3) = 1001.0986.

Example 5. -inf entries drop out cleanly, as zero-probability terms.

double ninf = -std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({ninf, ninf, 2.0}).logsumexp(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=2.0000

Example 6. The backward pass is the softmax of the input.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

x.logsumexp(0).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.090030573, 0.24472847, 0.66524096]

Those are softmax([1, 2, 3]), and they sum to 1.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Reach for logsumexp() rather than x.exp().sum().log() whenever the values can be large. The naive form overflows to inf.

  • The no-argument form reduces everything; pass dim to reduce a single axis.

  • All--inf input reduces to -inf; a NaN anywhere in the reduced axis propagates.

  • Floating-point input.

Summary¶

logsumexp(x) is a stable log(sum(exp(x))) reduction:

  • shifts by the max so nothing overflows

  • dim / keepdim behave like the other reductions

  • differentiable, backward is softmax(x) along the reduced axis

See Also¶

  • Series::logcumsumexp: the running (prefix) version along an axis.

  • Series::logaddexp: the two-argument, broadcasting form.

  • Series::sum: the plain additive reduction.
